Heavy work that formerly belonged to men only is being done by girls. The ice girls are delivering ice on a route and their work requires brawn as well as the partriotic ambition to help." Photo taken September 16, 1918. National Archives. Last week we talked about the ice harvest during WWI, so I thought this week we would visit this amazing photo you've perhaps seen making the rounds of the internet. ​Housed at the National Archives, the title reads, "Girls deliver ice. Heavy work that formerly belonged to men only is being done by girls. The ice girls are delivering ice on a route and their work requires brawn as well as the patriotic ambition to help." Two fresh-faced White girls wearing generous overalls and shirts with the sleeves rolled up, their hair tucked under newsboy caps, strain with ice tongs to lift an enormous block of what appears to be natural ice. As the ice appears to be resting on the ground, it's unclear if this photo was posed or not.Large, irregular chunks of ice dot the road beside them, and the open back of an ice wagon is in the background. This photo is a perfect illustration of two major needs of the First World War colliding. One was the huge shift in labor that occurred during the war. With so many men conscripted to the fields of France, it fell to women to enter the workforce, including in fields that typically required "brawn" as well as "patriotic ambition." But while working in fields and factories is understandable to our modern concepts of labor, the idea of ice delivery is maybe not quite so easy to understand. Prior to the 1940s, the majority of Americans refrigerated their foods with ice. If you've ever heard your grandma call the refrigerator an "ice box," she's likely either experienced one, or the term has stayed in usage in her family enough for her to adopt it. An ice box is literally a box in which an enormous block of ice is placed at the top. The cold air and meltwater fall around the container below, in which perishable foods and beverages were placed to keep cool. Although not as cold as modern refrigerators (which hover at around 39-40 degrees F), ice boxes were considerably cooler than cellars and helped prevent meat and dairy products from spoiling, kept vegetables fresh, and even allowed for iced drinks. But, as you can see in the photo, the ice tended to melt fairly quickly. So new ice had to be delivered at least once a week. [![Image 16: Picture](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/uploads/2/5/8/6/25860210/editor/new-york-ice-trade-colour-wikimedia.jpg?1673922153)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:New_York_Ice_trade_colour.jpg) "Ice Trade in New York" from "Harper's Weekly," August 30, 1884. Colorized. Wikimedia Commons. ​This colorized illustration from Harper's Weekly shows how the ice was delivered in New York City. It would be taken from enormous ice houses on the Hudson River, storing ice harvested in winter, loaded onto barges, which were towed by steamboats down the Hudson River to New York City, then unloaded from the barges onto shore (or onto transatlantic steamboats) and from shore onto innumerable ice wagons, which would then deliver for commercial or household use. The constant flow of deliveries - sometimes multiple times a day and by competing delivery companies - made for a very inefficient system, especially when it came to labor. Ice was not the only industry using inefficient deliveries - greengrocers, butchers, dry goods salesmen, and milk deliveries also competed with ice for road space and orders. The First World War's impact on labor and the Progressive Era's obsession with efficiency helped to reduce the number of delivery wagons (later trucks) and also the frequency of deliveries, especially to individual households. Nevertheless, efficiency could only go so far. People were still needed to do the labor, and these girls fit the bill. Ice delivery was not a nice trade - it was cold, wet, and often dirty. The work involved endless heavy lifting. Most ice men delivered ice by using the tongs to clamp down on the block (usually a sight smaller than the one they're handling in the photo), and then sling it over his shoulder, resting on a leather pad to protect his shoulder from frostbite. The frequent deliveries to women alone at home inspired jokes (and [even songs](https://digitalcommons.library.umaine.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=https://www.google.com/&httpsredir=1&article=4884&context=mmb-vp)) similar to the milkman jokes of the 1950s. Perhaps that was why these young women went into the ice trade in 1918? Regardless, the photo was taken in September, 1918, just a few months before Armistice. It is doubtful these young ladies continued in the trade as many women, especially those working in difficult or lucrative jobs, were almost immediately displaced by returning soldiers. I don't know how this photo was used in the period, but perhaps it was used much in the same way we react to it today - applauding the strength and grit of the women who proved they could do the same work as a man. * * * [](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/store/p4/Tip_Jar.html) ## Tip Jar $1.00 - $20.00 [Support](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/store/p4/Tip_Jar.html)​​The Food Historian blog is supported by patrons on[Patreon!](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)Patrons help keep blog posts like this one free and available to the public.[Join us for awesome members-only content](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)like free digitized cookbooks from my personal collection, e-newsletter, and even snail mail from time to time! National Association of Ice Industries. Engineer. If you are a Patriot, If This Is Your Fight, Get Into It. Stop The Ammonia Leaks." National Archives. You may be wondering, what on earth do ammonia and engineers have to do with food history? Well, ammonia was one of the primary ingredients in creating artificial ice in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The poster above shows Uncle Sam brandishing a wrench, hand on the shoulder of an older engineer, who reclines in a chair reading the newspaper. One sheet of the newspaper has fallen to the floor, and we can make out "War" in the headline. In the background we can see the outlines of pipes and valves. The poster reads "ENGINEER - If you are a patriot, If this is your fight, Get Into It - Stop the Ammonia Leaks." The top of the poster indicates it was sponsored by both the United States Food Administration and the National Association of Ice Industries. Refrigeration was changing rapidly in the 1900s. Most of the country still refrigerated with "natural ice," or ice harvested in winter from freshwater sources like lakes and rivers. But "artificial ice," that is water frozen mechanically, was gaining ground. Artificial ice making factories had been around since the 1870s, but they were costly and inefficient, used primarily in warmer climes where shipping natural ice was too inefficient. The primary refrigerant in these factories was ammonia, which has explosive properties. In fact, ammonia is a primary component in making gunpowder and explosives, and obviously demand for its use went up exponentially when the U.S. joined the First World War in April of 1917. Ammonia cools through compression. Jonathan Reese in _[Before the Refrigerator: How We Used to Get Ice](https://amzn.to/3koYl9Z)_(_Amazon affiliate link_) explains the process: > The compression refrigeration cycle depends on the compressor forcing a refrigerant around a system of coils. A refrigerant is any substancethat can be used to draw heat away from an adjoining space, but some refrigerants worked much better than others. During the late nineteenth century, most American refrigerating machines used ammonia as their refrigerant. The main advantage of ammonia was that it was very efficient. Inother words, it has a very low vaporizing temperature (or boiling point) atwhich it will turn from a liquid into a gas. This means that it required lessenergy to propel it through the cycle and remove heat from whatever spaceor substance that the operator needed to become cold. If ammonia leakedthrough the pipes of these early machines (which it was prone to do),under certain circumstances it could even explode, as the New York packing house example described above illustrates.¹⁰ Most American refrigerating equipment manufacturers didn’t realize that until ammonia compres sion refrigeration systems had become extremely popular.¹¹ > > Like all mechanical refrigeration systems, ice machines of the late nineteenth century had four different components. First were the coils, wherethe refrigerant would absorb heat from the surrounding water. The largerthe area of direct contact between the coils and the area where the temperature was supposed to go down, the more heat could be transferred. Second came the compressor, which turned the gaseous refrigerant into a liquid and provided the power through the change in pressure that propelledthe refrigerant throughout the machine. Third was the condenser, wherethe refrigerant cooled and liquefied. The last component of an ice orrefrigeration machine was the expansion valve that regulated the readmission of the liquid into the pipes, where the process would begin again.A compressor is a cylinder with a piston inside of it. When the compressor filled with gas, the piston would contract. The expansion of thepiston eliminated the gas from the compressor and propelled it throughthe system. Compression began when the change in pressure that thecompressor created forced the gaseous form of the refrigerant into a liquid. After the refrigerant got carried through an expansion valve, the pressure dropped. When that happened, the refrigerant absorbed heat from theadjoining space. > > If the adjoining space was full of water, the water became ice. If the adjoining space was open, that space could be used for cold storage. Cold storage also increased in use during the First World War, and refrigerated railroad cars, which helped drive agricultural specialization in fruits and vegetables around the country (Georgia peaches, Florida oranges, Michigan cherries, New York apples, and California's salad bowl), depended on ice for refrigeration and cooling. Ice was the invisible ingredient in the nation's food system. The National Association of Ice Industries was founded in August, 1917 in Chicago, IL as ice harvesters, producers, and distributors gathered at a conference. Realizing the importance of the ice trade in food preservation and conservation, the association vowed to cooperate with the government as part of the war effort. The conference proceedings were reported in _[Refrigerating World](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Refrigerating\_World/Jig6AQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22National+Association+of+Ice+Industries%22&pg=RA8-PA13&printsec=frontcover),_ the industry's trade journal,in the September, 1917 issue.​ [![Image 18: Picture](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/uploads/2/5/8/6/25860210/refrigerating-world-september-1917-national-organization-of-ice-industries-google-books_orig.png)](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Refrigerating_World/Jig6AQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22National+Association+of+Ice+Industries%22&pg=RA8-PA13&printsec=frontcover) "National Association of Ice Industries: New Organization Formed at Patriotic Gathering at Chicago. To Co-operate With the Government," article detailing conference proceedings in "Refrigerating World," September, 1917 issue. Click to read whole article. In addition to forming the National Association of Ice Industries on the second day of the conference, the attendees also discussed convincing farmers of the benefits of cold storage and encouraging them to construct ice houses on their farms, of convincing the public that using ice and refrigeration would reduce food waste and save money, and finally of reducing inefficiencies in delivery, including advocating for one delivery service making one delivery per day to prevent competing delivery companies from wasting manpower, horsepower, and ice. Wartime not only necessitated the conservation of ammonia, but also gave the natural ice industry a boost. Already in decline due to concerns about polluted waterways, [the natural ice industry was encouraged to revive](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesdays-ice-is-needed) as another way to conserve ammonia and the fuel that powered the steam engines and electric motors that powered the refrigerating process. The revival would ultimately be short-lived. The end of the First World War all but ended the natural ice industry. As refrigerants became abundant again and energy prices came back down, the demand for artificial ice went up. The advent of electric home refrigerators in the 1920s ultimately signaled the end of the household ice box, and the deliveries that went with it. **Read More:** _The Amazon affiliate links below help support The Food Historian_ * _[Harvest of the Cold Months: The Social History of Ice and Ices](https://amzn.to/3iEWttw)_ by Elizabeth David (1995) * _[Refrigeration Nation: A History of Ice, Appliances, and Enterprise in America](https://amzn.to/3XeJRIl)_ by Jonathan Reese (2016) * _[Before the Refrigerator: How We Used to Get Ice](https://amzn.to/3XiizRr)_ by Jonathan Reese (2018) * _[Cooling the Tropics: Ice, Indigeneity, and Hawaiian Refreshment](https://amzn.to/3Xyu86W)_ by Hi'ilei Julia Kawehipuaakahaopulani Hobart (2022) * * * [](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/store/p4/Tip_Jar.html) ## Tip Jar $1.00 - $20.00 [Support](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/store/p4/Tip_Jar.html)​​The Food Historian blog is supported by patrons on[Patreon!](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)Patrons help keep blog posts like this one free and available to the public.[Join us for awesome members-only content](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)like free digitized cookbooks from my personal collection, e-newsletter, and even snail mail from time to time! [1 Comment](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesday-stop-ammonia-leaks#comments) ## [World War Wednesday: Apple Indian Pudding Recipe (1917)](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesday-apple-indian-pudding-recipe-1917) 11/9/2022 [0 Comments](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesday-apple-indian-pudding-recipe-1917#comments) [![Image 19: Picture](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/uploads/2/5/8/6/25860210/published/sunmaid-indian-pudding-ad-1918.jpg?1662598037)](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/category/world-war-wednesdays) Advertisement for Sun-maid Raisins, c. 1918, one of several from this time period. This one features Indian pudding with raisins as the headline image. Public domain. I don't remember when I first encountered "Indian pudding." Derived from the Colonial name for cornmeal - "Indian meal" - it's an iconic dish of New England, though it isn't often made anymore. Combining Indigenous foodways, European cooking techniques, and molasses, a ubiquitous sweetener made cheap by the brutal labor of enslaved Africans, Indian pudding reflected the kind of stick-to-your-ribs cooking common in the Colonial period when people ate less frequently and engaged in harder labor, and with less access to heating than they do today. ​The above advertisement by Sun-maid Raisins from 1918 is a good illustration of this. "Note How Plain Foods Become Enticing," the ad reads, showing how Indian Pudding could be spiced up with raisins, and then goes on to show just how inexpensive raisins were. Historically, raisins were rather expensive, and had to be stoned (remove the seeds) by hand, a labor-intensive step that continued until the early 20th century. By the time Sun-maid is advertising in 1918, you no longer had to stone raisins - they came seedless. Clearly Sun-maid was trying to convince people that raisins were a more economical purchase than previously believed. Also, the use of Indian Pudding to illustrate the "plain foods" shows how it was viewed by most Americans at that time - plain, cheap, and filling. Indian pudding also fit nicely into rationing suggestions to use less sugar, refined white flour, and fats. With its ingredients of cornmeal and molasses, Indian pudding fit the bill. I first ran across a recipe for Apple Indian Pudding when researching the history of the [Farm Cadets in New York State](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesday-farm-cadets). The article right next to it was about the establishment of the Farm Cadet Corps under the State Military Training commission. Published in the _Buffalo Evening News_ on April 19, 1917, just two weeks after the United States entered the war, it was included as part of a column called "Lucy Lincoln's Talks" and was one of many recipes. Although the United States Food Administration was not yet formed and no rationing recommendations had been issued, President Wilson had been publicly discussing the role of food in the war effort. Throughout the First World War, the United States Food Administration and home economists hearkened back to the Colonial period for several reasons. First, it appealed to Americans' sense of patriotism. Following the American Civil War, Northern reformers made a concerted effort to re-unite the nation and define what it meant to be American. Thanks to the unconscious bias of white supremacy, that idea became closely connected to New England and the mythology around the Pilgrims and the founding of the nation (despite the fact that Spanish Florida, Virginia, parts of Canada, and even New York had been settled earlier). Second, hearkening back to the Colonial period allowed ration supporters to encourage the substitution of non-rationed food items like cornmeal and molasses which had deep Colonial roots, for rationed foods like refined white flour and refined white sugar, which were needed for the war effort. Third, these ingredients were often very inexpensive. By connecting them to the honored founders of the country, food reformers could convince middle and upper class people to eat what may have been previously only associated with the poor and working class, in the name of patriotism. Despite the lack of actual rationing recommendations at this point, the recipe for Apple Indian Pudding would have fit very nicely into the requirements. It used cornmeal, which saved wheat. It used molasses and apples for sweetener, which saved sugar. It used two quarts of milk, which would help use up the [milk surplus](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/world-war-wednesday-eat-more-milk) and add protein.It was also extremely inexpensive and filling, which meant it had appeal for folks on a budget or with large families. The recipe does, however, call for 1/3 cup of butter, which would become one of the recommended ration items in just a few months. ## Apple Indian Pudding Recipe [![Image 20: Picture](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/uploads/2/5/8/6/25860210/published/apple-indian-pudding-buffalo-evening-news-4-19-1917.jpg?1667773327)](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/category/world-war-wednesdays) Recipe for Apple Indian Pudding, published in the "Buffalo Evening News," Buffalo, NY, on April 19, 1917. I have made Indian Pudding before for a talk, and it's lovelier than you'd think. Here's the original recipe: _"Scald 2 quarts of milk in a double boiler. Sprinkle in 1 cup of Indian meal, stirring all the time, and cook 45 minutes, stirring frequently. Remove from the fire, add 1/3 cup of butter, 1 cup of molasses, 2 teaspoons of salt, 1/2 teaspoon each of ginger and grated nutmeg, and 1 quart of pared, cored, and quartered apples. Turn into a buttered baking dish and bake three hours in a slow oven."_ And here's a modern translation: 8 cups (or a half gallon) whole milk 1 cup cornmeal 1/3 cup butter 1 cup molasses 2 teaspoons salt 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger 1/2 teaspoon grated fresh nutmeg 3-4 apples Preheat the oven to 300 F. In a double boiler or heavy-bottomed pot, heat the milk, but do not boil. Once hot, slowly whisk in the cornmeal and cook, stirring frequently, for 30-45 mins or until the cornmeal is fully cooked and has absorbed the milk. Remove from heat and while hot, stir in the butter, molasses, salt, and spices. Peel, core, and slice the apples thickly. Stir the apple slices into the cornmeal mixture, and tip it all into a buttered glass or ceramic baking dish. Place in the oven and let bake for 3 hours, uncovered. Serve hot or warm plain (ration-friendly) or with vanilla ice cream or unsweetened liquid cream (not-so ration-friendly). Although the original recipe calls for quartered apples, most modern apples are very large, and a quarter might be too big, which is why I suggest slicing them instead. If you're in an area of the world that gets cold in the fall and winter, Apple Indian Pudding is the perfect, homey dessert to attempt on a day when you'll be puttering around the kitchen or the house all day. Pop some baked beans in with it if you really want a traditional New England supper (and a ration-friendly one!). It really does take three whole hours to bake (other versions included steaming like plum pudding), but the long, slow heat turns the normally crunchy cornmeal into melting softness. There's a reason why it's still [so popular in New England](https://newengland.com/today/food/desserts/puddings-custards/indian-pudding-2/). If you want to know more about the history of Indian Pudding, including how to make a historic recipe, check out my lecture below! Between social media ([Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/thefoodhistorian),[Instagram](http://www.instagram.com/preserveorperish),[Twitter](http://www.twitter.com/history_bites)) and this blog, I'll be sharing vintage Halloween content nearly every day this month! [![Image 21: Picture](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/uploads/2/5/8/6/25860210/halloween-san-diego-union-oct-25-1942_orig.jpg)](https://www.thefoodhistorian.com/blog/category/world-war-wednesdays) Cartoon published in the "San Diego Union," October 25, 1942. Ghosts of Emperor Hirohito of Japan, Adolph Hitler of Germany, and Benito Mussolini say in unison, "Do something destructive this Halloween - you'll be helping us -" to a teenaged boy in an alley. A black cat on the fence behind him says, "You're an AMERICAN - don't listen to those goons!" Trick or treating today is usually about young children, costumes, and lots of candy. In many communities, it's over by 8 or 9 pm. But historically, trick or treating was more about the tricks than the treats. Going door to door threatening tricks if treats were not offered instead is very old, but has deeper roots in association with Christmas than with Halloween. Despite the tradition's age, going door to door for treats on Halloween was not widely practiced in the United States until the 20th century. The pranks, however, were popular among teenaged boys. From the relatively harmless pranks like soaping car windows and placing furniture on porch roofs to the destructive ones like slashing tires, breaking windows, egging houses, and starting fires in the streets, pranks were common in communities across the country. The war changed all that. Halloween, 1942 was the first since the United States entered the war in December, 1941. Across the nation, newspapers published warnings to would-be prankers that destructive acts of the past would no longer be tolerated. This one, published on [October 30, 1942 in _The Corning Daily Observer_](https://newscomwc.newspapers.com/image/835153473/?terms=halloween%20pranks&pqsid=SuqL_fLNy7zD2AYbIuUsug%3A2600000%3A272515262&match=1)in Corning, California, was typical of other messages other newspapers: _**"Hallowe'en Pranks Are Out For the Duration"** "The destructive Hallowe'en pranks of breaking fences, stealing gates, deflating auto tires, ringing door bells to disturb sleepers, soaping windows, and all other forms of the removal or destruction of buildings or property are definitely out and forbidden on Hallowe'en night, according to word from Corning city officials. "Supplies are needed for national defense and are too scarce to permit misuse. "Word comes from Washington that individuals committing such offense shall be prosecuted as saboteurs and be treated accordingly. "Corning officials state that there will be no fooling about this matter this year and anyone contemplating 'having fun' will be treated with severely."_ The newspaper cartoon above, published in the _San Francisco Union_ on October 25, 1942, illustrates just this sentiment. In it, the ghosts of Japanese Emperor Hirohito, German Chancellor Adolph Hitler, and Italian fascist Prime Minister Benito Mussolini egg on a young boy hanging out in a dark back alleyway. "Do something destructive this Halloween - - - You'll be helping us - " they tell him. On the high fence behind the boy stands a black cat, back arched in anger, silhouetted by a full moon. He says to the boy, "You're an**American**- - Don't listen to those goons!" Conflating Halloween pranks with sabotage and aiding the Axis powers was no joke. The November, 1942 newspapers feature stories of pranksters waking sleeping war workers, scaring their neighbors by setting off air raid bells, and causing car accidents by leaving debris in the roads. Several ended up in court, and some got buckshot wounds from angry homeowners for their efforts. Wartime propaganda like this was common - caricatures of the Axis leaders showed up frequently in newspapers, cartoons, and propaganda posters. For Halloween, they made convenient bogeymen. World War II was the beginning of the end of Halloween tricks. Although more innocuous pranks like egging houses and cars and toilet-papering trees and porches continued to be hallmarks of Halloween mischief, the days of fires in the streets, broken windows, and other real crimes were largely in the past. Communities that had previously celebrated Halloween with private parties at home, shifted to more public events like parades, community dances, and trick-or-treating geared toward small children getting treats rather than teenagers engaging in tricks. **Further Reading** If you'd like to learn more about Halloween during World War II, check out these additional resources: * "[Halloween in Wartime](http://www.sandiegoyesterday.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/Halloween-in-Wartime.pdf)" from San Diego Yesterday * "[Halloween on the Home Front](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/halloween-in-1940s-home-front)" National WWII Museum * "[Have Fun, But Remember the War](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/blog/general/have-fun-but-remember-the-war-halloween-during-world-war-ii)" Heinz History Center * "[How Donald Duck and Peanuts Saved Trick-or-Treating](https://www.history.com/news/how-donald-duck-and-peanuts-saved-trick-or-treating)" History.com​ * * * ​​The Food Historian blog is supported by patrons on[Patreon!](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)Patrons help keep blog posts like this one free and available to the public.[Join us for awesome members-only content](http://www.patreon.com/thefoodhistorian)like free digitized cookbooks from my personal collection, e-newsletter, and even snail mail from time to time! PRESIDENT'S  LETTER  OF  TRANSMITTAL

To  THE  CONGRESS  OF  THE  UNITED  STATES  OF  AMERICA:

I  am  transmitting  herewith  the  sixth  report  to  Congress  on  UNRRA
operations  for  the  quarter  ending  December  31,  1945.
During  this  quarter,  while  UNRRA’s  shipments  reached  unprecedented
figures,  recipient  countries  experienced  unprecedented  needs.  Crop  failures
resulted  in  the  continuance  of  near  famine  conditions.  The  hardships  of
winter  were  imminent.
At  year’s  end,  moreover,  critical  shortages  (notably  of  wheat,  fats,  meat
for  Europe,  and  of  rice  for  China)  threatened  execution  of  even  the  limited
relief  program  that  had  been  planned.  For  millions  survival  was,  and  still
is,  the  issue,  and  for  UNRRA  the  challenge  to  be  met.  World  recovery
still  remains  a  formidable  task.
Only  concerted  action  by  the  United  Nations  (and,  primarily,  of  the
producing  countries)  can,  even  at  this  date,  avert  the  prolongation  of
emergency  conditions  throughout  the  world.  Now,  more  than  ever,  inten-
sified  efforts  to  match  need  with  supply,  are  required  of  us.  We  must  not
fail.  For  our  continued  participation  in  UNRRA  marks  the  fulfillment  of
a  pledge  and  the  discharge  of  a  debt  to  those  who,  beyond  the  common
sacrifice  of  life  and  material  resources,  endured  the  devastation  and  bru-
talities  that  we  were  spared.  Conscience  alone  demands  that  we  meet  the
full  measure  of  our  obligation.
But  prudence  and  self-interest  no  less  dictate  our  policy.  Neither  peace
nor  prosperity  can  be  assured  to  us  while  famine,  disease  and  destitution
deprive  others  of  the  means  to  live,  let  alone  to  prosper.  Relief and  rehabil-
itation  are  paramount  necessities  for  that  world  recovery  which  is  a  primary
objective  of  our  national  policy.  They  provide  the  best  insurance  against
social  chaos  and  moral  disintegration  and  the  surest  guarantee  for  the
growth  of  democratic  modes  of  thought  and  action.  The  emergency,
which  UNRRA  was  designed  to  meet,  continues.  The  months  immedi-
ately  ahead  are  critical.
While  ours  is  the  largest  contribution  to  UNRRA’s  funds,  it  is  matched
by  like,  proportionate  contributions  of  30  other  nations.  This  gives  sig-
nificance  to  UNRRA  altogether  beyord  the  relief  that  it  provides.  In
UNRRA  the  United  Nations  have  created  the  first  international  operating
agency  through  which  to  test  and  to  perfect  our  powers  of  cooperation.
Such  powers  are  not  inborn.  They  are  cultivated,  by  constant  exercise
and  the  progressive  enlargement  of  mutual  experience.  In  UNRRA  a
precedent  has  been  created  that  may  prove  a  landmark  in  our  progress
toward  solidarity  and  common  action  by  the  nations  of  the  world.

Chapter  1
WAR'S  AFTERMATH
The  “cease  fire”  order  which,  for  most  Americans,  signalled  the  resump-
tion  of  peacetime  pursuits,  carried  a  sterner  message  to  the  people  of Europe
and  the  Far  East.  For  them  it  meant  the  redepleyment  of  their  moral  and
material  resources  against  new  enemies.  War  did  not  so  much  end  as
change  front.  Men  entered  on  a  struggle  with  conditions  described  300
years  ago:
“In  such  condition  there  is  no  place  for  industry,  because  the  fruit  thereof
is  uncertain,  and  consequently,  no  culture  of  the  earth,  no  navigation,  nor
use  of  the  commodities  that  may  be  imported  by  sea,  no  commodious  build-
ing,  no  instruments  of  moving  and  removing  such  things  as  require  much
force;  and  which  is  worst  of  all,  continual  fear  and  danger  of death;  and  the
life  of  man  solitary,  poor,  nasty,  brutish  and  short.”
The  summer  months,  preceding  the  period  here  under  review,  brought,
it  is  true,  brief  respite  of  clement  weather.  But  they  brought  little  else  of
comfort.  As,  throughout  1945,  men  and  women  strove  to  repair  the
damages  of  war,  the  full  significance  of  the  break-down  of  all  the  sinews  of
organized  society  became  increasingly  apparent.  :
Starvation,  plague,  exposure,  isolation—these  and  other  ills  could  have
been  dealt  with  singly.  But  collectively  they  made  for  liabilities  in  which
the  total  was  more  than  the  sum  of  all  the  parts.  Their  needs  and  their
distresses  inter-acted,  one  aggravating  another  and  increasing  their  over-all
predicament.

Manpower  Short
In  and  out  of  government,  manpower  was  short.  In  Yugoslavia,  every
seventh  person  had  been  killed,  in  Greece,  one  man  in  8,  in  Poland,  one
in  6.  The  training,  too,  of  skilled  personnel  had  come  to  a  virtual  stand-
still  during  the  war  years.
Equipment  Destroyed
In  industry  and  on  the  farm,  loss  of  equipment  aggravated  the  man-
power  shortage.  In  Czechoslovakia,  25,000  citizens  responded  to  a  call
to  man  the  mines.  Bankers  and  clerks,  doctors  and  lawyers,  hauled  out
the  coal  with  hand  and  shovel.  In  Yugoslavia,  absence  of  ploughs  and

5

tractors  threatened  food  supplies.  A  peasant  woman  ‘ploughed’  a  whole
field,  singlehanded,  with  an  axe.  2,

No  Trucks,  No  Trains
In  the  Silesian  mines,  machinery  was  intact,  but  here,  as  elsewhere,
another  ill  assailed  them.  Freight  cars  and  trucks  were  lacking.  Coal  at
the  pithead  stood  for  sale  at  360  zlotys.  In  faraway  Warsaw  it  fetched
8,000  zlotys.  Wheat,  harvested  by  hand  with  superhuman  effort,  lay
rotting  for  lack  of  transport  to  carry  it  to  areas  where  people  starved.

No  Food,  No  Clothes,  No  Shelter
Lack  of  shelter,  of  food  and  clothing  likewise  added  to  cumulative  strains,
taking  their  toll  in  sickness,  debility  and  death.  In  Yugoslavia,  one-half  a
million  homes  were  destroyed  (one  Bosnian  village,  during  the  war,  had
changed  hands  56  times).  In  Italy  400,000  people  were  without  shelter;
in  Warsaw  men  and  boys  searched  the  rubble  of  the  ruins  for  scraps  of
roofing  paper  with  which  to  cover  their  feet;  in  Greece,  more  than  half  the
population  were  still  without  minimum  clothing  needs..  From  Doboj,  in
Yugoslavia,  the  Germans  had  removed  even  swaddling  clothes,  as  padding
for  their  tanks.  Towns  and  villages  all  across  Europe  told  the  same  story,
“Nema  mishta”—there  is  nothing.

The  Crops  Fail
And,  as  though  war  and  its  aftermath  were  not  enough,  nature  conspired
to  thwart  men’s  first  painful  efforts  at  recovery.  Country  after  country  in
the  Mediterranean  basin  experienced  the  worst  drought  in  decades.  Har-
vests  fell  short  of  prewar  levels  by  50-60-70  percent.  Shortage  piled  on
shortage.  Prices  sky-rocketed  and  bewildered  men  and  women  fingered
money  that  had  lost  its  value.
Winter  Ahead
Conditions  such  as  these  persisted  into  late  summer  and  fall.  Some
became  aggravated.  And  ahead  was  winter.  The  first  frosts  came.
Villagers  in  Yugoslavia  kept  indoors  for  lack  of  footwear,  or  borrowed
from  a  neighbor.  Hospitals  had  no  heat.  In  Poland,  in  November,  a
train  steamed  in,  bringing  1,500  people  from  the  eastern  provinces.  They
had  travelled  in  open  cars  at  12  degrees  below  zero.  Six  children  froze
to  death.  In  Greece  mountain  villages  faced  the  prospect  of  complete
isolation  from  the  world  until  the  spring.  Everywhere  men  remained
preoccupied  with  bare  survival.  Recovery  was  a  mere  dream,  a  hope
deferred.

‘As  in  the  west,  so  in  the  east.  In  Hankow,  the  Chinese  Chicago,  power
companies  and  factories  are  deathly  still.  Hands,  once  raised  to  cheer

Such  is  the  partial  story  of  the  world’s  predicament.  =  No  record  in  history
survives  of  ruin  and  distress  so  universal.  F igures  that  seem  astronomical
(of  tonnages  and  dollar  values  of  relief  supplied)  dwindle  to  insignificance
beside  the  desolation  and  the  need.  These,  like  the  record  which  follows,
represent  only  the  first,  partial  contribution  made,  through  UNRRA,  by

still  in  the  throes  of  the  aftermath  of  war.

Chapter  2
ACHIEVEMENTS  OF  THE  QUARTER!

Before  April  1945  UNRRA'’s  activities  were  mainly  limited  to  the  advance
procurement  of  supplies  and  the  assembling  and  training  of  its  staff.  Ship-
ments  were  negligible.  Even  in  the  first  6  months  of  its operations  in  the
field  (from  April  to  September),  little  more  than  palliative  measures  had
proved  possible.  Relief  goods  were,  in  large  measure,  still  in  short  supply.
Shipping  remained  heavily  committed  to  military  needs.  As  the  fall  came,
time  pressed.  Hungry  and  homeless,  ill-clad,  ill-shod,  and  destitute—
millions  looked  with  dread  toward  winter’s  approach.  The  peak  of  crisis
soared  immediately  ahead.
It  was  to  this  emergency  that UNRRA  addressed  itself  in  the  last  quarter
of  1945.  With  supplies  and  shipping  now,  at  last,  more  readily  available,
the  relief  program  began  to  hit  its  stride.

Shipments  Increase

UNRRA  shipments  in  October  were  estimated  at  566,300  gross  long
tons,  a  record,  to  date.  458,600  tons  were  moved  from  the  Western
Hemisphere  alone,  the  bulk  of them  from  the  United  States.  In  November,
a  fresh  record  was  achieved.  Shipments  exceeded  those  even  of October  by
20  percent,  amounting  to  an  estimated  689,500  gross  long  tons.  523,080
tons  moved  out  of  ports  in  the  Western  Hemisphere,  the  bulk  of  them  from
the  United  States.  .
Owing,  chiefly,  to  shortage  of  ships  crews  in  the  United  States,  December
shipments  which,  it  had  been  hoped,  would  top  the  million  mark,  fell
short  of  expectations.  562,100  tons  were  shipped,  bringing  the  cumulative
total  for  the  year  to  3,959,300  tons.  The  last  quarter  of  the  year  ranked
first  in  the  volume  and  the  scale  of  the  relief provided,  though  this  continued
far  short  of  requirements  in  regard  to  some  essential  commodities.  World
shortages  and  problems  of  transportation  and  delivery  still  hampered
achievement  of  goals  set.

Army  Surpluses  Avert  Disaster
Shipments  from  overseas  were  supplemented  by  the  timely  release  of
large  Army  surpluses.  UNRRA  has  bought  huge  stocks  of  surplus  supplies
which  otherwise  might  have  found  no  market  or  might  have  depressed
markets  if  dumped  in  the  United  States.  American  contributions  to
UNRRA  have  thus  indirectly  helped  American  farmers,  workers,  and
employers.?  Among  resulting  benefits  was  the  supply  of  a  great  quantity
of  trucks  to  countries  where  lack  of  transport  had  seriously  delayed  provi-
sion  of  relief.  Shipments  now  not  only  reached  their  ports  of  destination,
but,  in  increasing  quantities,  were  delivered  to  those  who  stood  in  need
of  them.  As  transport  became  available,  warehouses  began  at  last  to
disgorge  their  congested  supplies.  One  of  the  most  tantalizing  bottle-necks
to  date  was  being  gradually  eliminated.

received  invaluable  support  from  the  contributions  of  voluntary  agencies
throughout  the  United  States.  These  voluntary  supplies  ranged  from

The  Two  Concurrent  Goals

The  main  objectives  of  the  quarter  were  two-fold—relief  from  the  ex-
tremes  of  present  need,  and  provision  for  the  future,  means  for  the  repair
of  industries  contributing  directly  to  relief  needs  and  for  the  recovery  of
agriculture  and  the  consequent  curtailment  of UNRRA’s  forward  liabilities.
The  more  and  the  quicker  men  helped  themselves,  the  less  and  the  shorter
the  need  for  external  assistance.
From  the  Western  Hemisphere,  food,  the  dominant,  immediate  need,
outstripped  by  far  all  other  shipments—in  October,  363,500  tons,  in Novem-
ber,  435,400  tons,  in  December,  364,000  tons.  Industrial  and  agricultural
rehabilitation  ranked  second.  Coal,  raw  materials,  and  essential  machinery
were  shipped;  tools  for  the  farmer,  tractors  and  ploughs,  basic  necessities
for  the  achievement  of  self-help  by  people  shorn  of  almost  everything  but
the  will  to  work  and  the  courage  to  survive.  Provisions  not  only  for  the  day
but  for  the  morrow—safest  insurance  against  the  unending  continuance  of
relief.  Shipment  of  these  supplies  conformed  to  a  plan  for  balanced  pro-
vision  of  relief  and  rehabilitation  supplies.  It  had  been  hoped  that,  by
the  end  of  1945,  increasing  emphasis  might  be  placed  on  the  latter.  But
between  August  and  December,  things  took  a  turn  for  the  worse.  Unan-
ticipated  world  shortages  of  wheat,  and  continuing  shortage  of  fats  and
oils  imperilled  the  relief  program.  The  continuing  urgency  of  the  demands
for  food,  fuel  and  transportation  necessitated  the  curtailment  of  supplies
of  raw  material  and  equipment  for  the  rehabilitation  of  agriculture  and
industry.  The  crisis  of  survival  was  prolonged.  Hope  of  recovery  was
again  deferred.

Gains  of  the  Quarter  Deferred

The  gains  of  the  quarter  were,  nevertheless,  decisive.  Millions  live  who,
but  for  UNRRA,  would  have  died.  The  suffering  of  further  millions  was
mitigated  by  the  provision  of  food  and  clothing,  shelter,  and  medicine.
The  importance,  moreover,  of what  has  been  averted  is  as  great  as  that  of
what  has  been  achieved.  Little  remarked,  but  of  high  significance,  is  the
total  absence  throughout  Europe  of any widespread  epidemics.  The  contrast
with  the  situation  at  the  end  of  World  War  I,  1914-1918,  is  striking.  Condi-
tions, widely  prevalent  in  almost  every  country,  were  an  open  invitation  to  in-
fection  and  the  spread  of disease.  Again  and  again,  UNRRA’s  medical  staff
~  has  helped  to  scotch  it  at  its  inception,  where  necessary,  flying  supplies  of
antitoxin,  DDT,  etc.,  by  plane  to  the  point  of  danger.  UNRRA  has
organized  the  largest  international  medical  relief  operation  in  history.  In
November  1945  there  were  800  UNRRA  physicians  and  nurses  at  work
in  Europe.
Pure  gain,  too,  has  been  the  steadily  increasing  delivery  of  rehabilitation
supplies.  While  these  have  not  always  shown  immediate  results,  they  will
earn  rich  dividends  as,  in  succeeding  months,  native  industries  increase
their  output  of basic  essential  supplies  and  the volume  of internal  trade  and  of
employment  increases,  thus  progressively  curtailing  UNRRA’s  burden  of
providing  help  from  outside  sources.  Already  countries  like  Poland  and
Czechoslovakia  have  produced  surpluses  which  they  have  made  available
for  the  relief  of  suffering  in  other  European  countries.  While  still  excep-
tional,  this  reciprocity  suggests  a  hopeful  trend.  Rewarding  dividends  will
likewise  be  paid  as,  in  springtime,  farmers  avail  themselves  of  tools  and  of
equipment  shipped  earlier  to  secure  spring  sowing.

UNRRA  Assumes  New  Responsibilities

The  above  record,  moreover,  covers  only  countries  already  in  receipt  of
substantial  aid.  Side  by  side  with  increased  provision  for  them,  planning
proceeded  for  a  significant  extension  of  UNRRA'’s  operations.  With  the
opening  of  ports  and  the  release  of  army  surpluses  in  the  Far  East,  a  huge
program  for  China  got  under  way.
Planning  likewise  went  ahead  for  the  extension  of  UNRRA'’s  services
to  the  two  Soviet  Republics  whose  request  for  assistance  had  been  approved.

Victims  of  a  peculiarly  tragic  fate  are  the  so-called  displaced  persons  of
Europe  and  the  Far  East.  During  the  war,  millions  of  men,  women,  and
children  were  torn  from  their  homes  and  scattered  like  chaff  across  three
continents,  either  as  refugees  or  as  impressed  slave  laborers  of  the  Axis
powers.  In  the  three  western  zones  of  occupied  Germany  alone,  they
numbered  over  6  million.  Hundreds  of  thousands  were  found  in  Italy
and  Austria,  thousands  more  in  Albania,  Greece,  the  Dodecanese  Islands,
Egypt,  Palestine,  Cyprus,  Ethiopia,  the  Belgian  Congo,  Tanganyika,  in
China,  and  the  Philippines.  In  enemy  territory,  once  their  usefulness  as
slave  laborers  ceased,  they  were  left  to  fend  for  themselves.  Many  were
starving,  ill-clothed  and  sick.  All  were  deprived  of  help  from  friends  and
neighbors  or  of  their  own  governments,  for  they  were  far  from  home.
One  of  UNRRA'’s  major  tasks  has  been  to  help  provide  for  these  victims

by  member  governments.
Included  in  this  total  are  sthottzations  of  $1.722,669,369  which  are
the  second  contributions  of  four  uninvaded  countries—the  United  States,
the  United  Kingdom,  Canada,  and  the  Dominican  Republic.  The  United

Congress  in  December,  in  addition  to  the  appropriation  of  $550  millions
representing  the  unpaid  balance  of  its  first  contribution.  Its  action  made
possible  the  resumption,  in  early  1946,  of  UNRRA’s  scheduled  program
to  meet  winter’s  crisis.  Canada  made  immediately  available  $22,522,522
of  its  second  authorized  contribution  of  $69,369,369.
Thirty  out  of  thirty-one  of  the  uninvaded  member  countries  have  either
paid  or  pledged  payment  of  their  first  contributions,  and  negotiations  are
in  progress  with  the  one  remaining  country.
Of  the  16  invaded  countries  12  have  paid  their  administrative  expenses
in  full;  2  have  paid  more  than  half,  and  the  remaining  2  (only  recently
admitted  to  membership)  have  not  yet  been  formally  requested  to  con-

undertaking  of  unprecedented  size  and  for  a  purpose  that  represents  that
larger  view  of  the  interdependence  of  peoples  on  which  the  future  peace
and  prosperity  of  the  world  hinges.

Chapter  5
THE  JOB  STILL  TO  BE  DONE

Shipments  in  the  last  quarter  of  1945,  surpassing  those  of  any  previous
quarter,  met  in  some  part  the  crisis  of  winter.  Survival  was  assured  to
millions  who  would  otherwise  have  died.  The  toll  of  life  among  those  to
whom  relief  came  too  late,  or  not  at  all,  cannot  be  reckoned.  In  China,
Austria,  and  the  two  Soviet  Republics,  it  was  certainly  considerable.
But  beyond  continuing  concern  with  the  provision  for  immediate  emer-
gency,  there  was  the  job  still  to  be  done.  While  shipment  of  ever-increas-
ing  quantities  of  goods  proceeded,  rapid  advance  was  made  toward  com-
pletion  of  the  program  of  supply  and  service  for  the  year  1946.  UNRRA’s
job  ahead  involved  at  once  larger  shipment  to  countries  already  served  and
the  extension  of  aid  to  new  areas  of  acute  distress.
For  countries  already  served,  provision,  in  time,  of  immediate  continuing
needs—of  food,  clothing,  medicine,  shelter  and  transportation,  and  of  the
“necessary  supplies  (seeds,  fertilizers,  farm  tools  and  machinery)  for  spring
sowing,  was  a  primary  objective.  Only  so  could  some  degree  of  self-
sufficiency  in  food  be  secured  for  peoples  who,  beyond  1946,  in  Europe,
.  and  beyond  March  31,  1947,  in  the  Far  East,  could  count  on  no  further
help  from  UNRRA.  Shipments  of  over  50,000  tons  of  seed  were  being
speeded  for  delivery  to  9  European  countries  and  to  China.  By  the  fulfill
ment  of  minimum  requirements  now,  UNRRA  diminished  the  necessity
for  direct  relief  in  the  future.
Like  provision  of supplies  for  industrial  rehabilitation  could  alone  prevent
a  relapse—even  collapse—of  the  various  national  economies,  or  an  indefi-
nite  protraction  of  economic  crisis  and  stagnation.  ‘Some  measure  of  self-
sufficiency  was  paramount  if  all  UNRRA’s  work  was  not  to  be  undone.
Rehabilitation  remained  harnessed  and  subservient  to  relief.  Even  par-
tial  restoration  of  prewar  standards  lay  far  beyond  either  the  defined  scope
of  UNRRA'’s  work,  the  period  of  its  operations  or  the  means  at  its  disposal.
If  only  the  litter,  so  to  speak,  could  be  removed,  men  might  begin  to  tread
again  the  long  road  toward  recovery.  But  by  December  a  new  emergency
arose  which  affected  the  character  of forward  shipments  and  the  whole  plan
for  the  gradual  transfer  of  emphasis  from  emergency  relief  to  shipment  of
rehabilitation  goods.  :

The  occasion  for  this  emergency  merits  brief  review.  In  mid-1945  it  was
estimated  that  wheat  supplies  would  be  ample  to  meet  the  needs  of  all
importing  countries.  But  by  August  the  picture  had  changed—for  the
worse.  As  the  result  of  disastrous  crop  failures  in  the  Mediterranean  basin,
receiving  countries  in  Europe  submitted  urgent  requests  for  increased  grain
shipments—for  Czechoslovakia  an  increase  of  200,000  tons,  for  Poland  a
forward  demand  ot  500,000  tons.  (Poland  normally  exports  surplus  grain.)
Moreover,  to  sustain  even  marginal  subsistence  in  urban  areas  throughout
Germany,  huge  increases  of wheat  supplies  were  needed.
Meanwhile  the  situation  was  further  aggravated  by  conditions  in  the
Far  East.  By  December,  rice  crops  were  known  to  be  gravely  disappointing.
With  rice  in  very  short  supply  (none  was  procurable  before  July  1945),
substantial  increase  of  wheat  shipments  to  China  became  paramount.
Eleventh  hour  advices,  further,  showed  need  for  importing  23  million  metric
tons  of rice  and/or  wheat  into Japan.
Thus  the  curve  of  demand  rose,  steeply  and  suddenly,  throughout  the
world.  These  enormous  additional  demands,  superimposed  on  crop  failures
in  Europe,  failure  of  the  Australian  crop  in  1944,  the  short  Argentine  crop
in  1944,  and  the  short  Canadian  crop  in  1945,  resulted  in  an  ugly  gap
between  import  requirements  and  available  supplies.
On  top  of  supply  shortages  came  shipping  and  transportation  shortages.
As,  on  oaqe  front,  the  situation  eased,  it  grew  worse  on  another.  Thus,  in
December,  shipments  of  all  sorts  from  the  United  States  were  seriously  cur-
tailed  by  lack  of  crews.  Grain  was  available.  Ships  were  not.  In  Jan-
uary,  when  ships  were  again  available,  transportation  troubles  prevented
grain  deliveries  to  dock  side.  Extreme  difficulties,  amounting  to  an  emer-
gency,  had  developed  in  moving  available  grain  from  the  producing  areas
throughout  the  world  to  ports  of  shipment.  At  the  close  of  the  year  there
was  in  sight  an  insufficiency  of  grain  to  meet  UNRRA’s  scheduled  re-
quirements  for  the  critical  month  of January  1946.  :
Thus,  at  the  close  of  1945,  instead  of  ample  provision  for  all,  a  wheat
deficit  was  indicated  of  195  million  bushels  (or  5%  million  long  tons)  for  the
period  ending June  1946.  The  incidence  of  crisis  would  be  greatest  between
January  and  June  1946.  The  requirements  of  invaded  countries  for  this
period  exceeded  the  supply  available  by  42  percent.
Shortage  of  fats  and  oils  were  even  worse,  but  here  the  trouble  was ss  of  long
standing.  During  the  second  half  of  1945,  UNRRA  was  able  to  ship  less
than  20  percent  of  the  requirements  in  countries  desperately  in  need.  For-
ward  prospects  suggested  small  improvement.
Thus  UNRRA’s  provision  for  emergency  relief,  to  avert  death  and  starva-
tion,  continued  a  first  charge  on  its  operations.  The  gradual  transfer  of
emphasis  to  provision  of  agricultural  and  industrial  rehabilitation  supplies
had  to  be  deferred.  UNRRA  coatinued  locked  in  a  struggle  to  secure  sur-
vival.  It  is  against  such  facts  and  figures  that  the  achievements  of  a  record
quarter  must  be  read.  For  they  provide  an  index,  not  only  of  the  limits  of

Byelorussian  and  Ukrainian  Soviet  Republics
Two  Soviet  Republics,  Byelorussia  and  the  Ukraine,  had  qualified  for
relief  assistance.  In  these  two  republics  the  destruction  of  war  had  reached
a  scale  never  before  known  in  history.  Twice  their  territories  were  a  battle-
ground—once  when  the  tide  of invasion  reached  to  Moscow  and  Stalingrad,
and  again  when  the  enemy  was  driven  out  by  the  victorious  Russian  armies.
The  enemy  removed  virtually  all  agricultural  machinery.  Livestock  was
decimated.  All  movable  stocks  of  food,  and  even  of  seeds,  were  removed.
City  after  city  was  totally  destroyed.  More  than  25,000,000  were  left
with  homes  completely  wrecked.
Forward  provision  was  made  during  the  quarter  for  relief  programs
amounting  to  $189  million  for  the  Ukraine  and  $61  million  for  Byelorussia.
First  shipments  began  before  the  end  of  the  year  (6  vessels  sailing  in  Novem-
ber,  7  in  December)  carrying  food  and  medical  supplies.  Formal  agree-
ments,  substantially  the  same  as  those  made  with  other  countries,  were
signed  on  December  18.  Under  these  agreements  the  two  Soviet  Republics
will  grant  to  UNRRA'’s  missions  privileges  and  immunities  similar  to
those  granted  to foreign  governments.  These  include  inviolability  of  the
mission’s  archives  and  premises,  exemption  from  taxes  and  immunity  from
suit  and  legal  process  with  regard  to  activities  exercised  within  the  scope
of  their  authority  under  the  agreement.  They  provide  also  for  complete
freedom  for  UNRRA  officials  to  observe  the  equitable  distribution  of
supplies  which  UNRRA  delivers.

On the third Wednesday of a particular month between 1935 and 1945 inclusive, more than one but fewer than ten freighters were sunk. In one of the first six months of the year before, one of these freighters left for another country, carrying 12 million pounds of relief supplies. How many quinine sulfate tablets were included in that freighter’s cargo, which also carried the items listed above?

PRESIDENT'S  LETTER  OF  TRANSMITTAL

To  THE  CONGRESS  OF  THE  UNITED  STATES  OF  AMERICA:

I  am  transmitting  herewith  the  sixth  report  to  Congress  on  UNRRA
operations  for  the  quarter  ending  December  31,  1945.
During  this  quarter,  while  UNRRA’s  shipments  reached  unprecedented
figures,  recipient  countries  experienced  unprecedented  needs.  Crop  failures
resulted  in  the  continuance  of  near  famine  conditions.  The  hardships  of
winter  were  imminent.
At  year’s  end,  moreover,  critical  shortages  (notably  of  wheat,  fats,  meat
for  Europe,  and  of  rice  for  China)  threatened  execution  of  even  the  limited
relief  program  that  had  been  planned.  For  millions  survival  was,  and  still
is,  the  issue,  and  for  UNRRA  the  challenge  to  be  met.  World  recovery
still  remains  a  formidable  task.
Only  concerted  action  by  the  United  Nations  (and,  primarily,  of  the
producing  countries)  can,  even  at  this  date,  avert  the  prolongation  of
emergency  conditions  throughout  the  world.  Now,  more  than  ever,  inten-
sified  efforts  to  match  need  with  supply,  are  required  of  us.  We  must  not
fail.  For  our  continued  participation  in  UNRRA  marks  the  fulfillment  of
a  pledge  and  the  discharge  of  a  debt  to  those  who,  beyond  the  common
sacrifice  of  life  and  material  resources,  endured  the  devastation  and  bru-
talities  that  we  were  spared.  Conscience  alone  demands  that  we  meet  the
full  measure  of  our  obligation.
But  prudence  and  self-interest  no  less  dictate  our  policy.  Neither  peace
nor  prosperity  can  be  assured  to  us  while  famine,  disease  and  destitution
deprive  others  of  the  means  to  live,  let  alone  to  prosper.  Relief and  rehabil-
itation  are  paramount  necessities  for  that  world  recovery  which  is  a  primary
objective  of  our  national  policy.  They  provide  the  best  insurance  against
social  chaos  and  moral  disintegration  and  the  surest  guarantee  for  the
growth  of  democratic  modes  of  thought  and  action.  The  emergency,
which  UNRRA  was  designed  to  meet,  continues.  The  months  immedi-
ately  ahead  are  critical.
While  ours  is  the  largest  contribution  to  UNRRA’s  funds,  it  is  matched
by  like,  proportionate  contributions  of  30  other  nations.  This  gives  sig-
nificance  to  UNRRA  altogether  beyord  the  relief  that  it  provides.  In
UNRRA  the  United  Nations  have  created  the  first  international  operating
agency  through  which  to  test  and  to  perfect  our  powers  of  cooperation.
Such  powers  are  not  inborn.  They  are  cultivated,  by  constant  exercise
and  the  progressive  enlargement  of  mutual  experience.  In  UNRRA  a
precedent  has  been  created  that  may  prove  a  landmark  in  our  progress
toward  solidarity  and  common  action  by  the  nations  of  the  world.

Chapter  1
WAR'S  AFTERMATH
The  “cease  fire”  order  which,  for  most  Americans,  signalled  the  resump-
tion  of  peacetime  pursuits,  carried  a  sterner  message  to  the  people  of Europe
and  the  Far  East.  For  them  it  meant  the  redepleyment  of  their  moral  and
material  resources  against  new  enemies.  War  did  not  so  much  end  as
change  front.  Men  entered  on  a  struggle  with  conditions  described  300
years  ago:
“In  such  condition  there  is  no  place  for  industry,  because  the  fruit  thereof
is  uncertain,  and  consequently,  no  culture  of  the  earth,  no  navigation,  nor
use  of  the  commodities  that  may  be  imported  by  sea,  no  commodious  build-
ing,  no  instruments  of  moving  and  removing  such  things  as  require  much
force;  and  which  is  worst  of  all,  continual  fear  and  danger  of death;  and  the
life  of  man  solitary,  poor,  nasty,  brutish  and  short.”
The  summer  months,  preceding  the  period  here  under  review,  brought,
it  is  true,  brief  respite  of  clement  weather.  But  they  brought  little  else  of
comfort.  As,  throughout  1945,  men  and  women  strove  to  repair  the
damages  of  war,  the  full  significance  of  the  break-down  of  all  the  sinews  of
organized  society  became  increasingly  apparent.  :
Starvation,  plague,  exposure,  isolation—these  and  other  ills  could  have
been  dealt  with  singly.  But  collectively  they  made  for  liabilities  in  which
the  total  was  more  than  the  sum  of  all  the  parts.  Their  needs  and  their
distresses  inter-acted,  one  aggravating  another  and  increasing  their  over-all
predicament.

Manpower  Short
In  and  out  of  government,  manpower  was  short.  In  Yugoslavia,  every
seventh  person  had  been  killed,  in  Greece,  one  man  in  8,  in  Poland,  one
in  6.  The  training,  too,  of  skilled  personnel  had  come  to  a  virtual  stand-
still  during  the  war  years.
Equipment  Destroyed
In  industry  and  on  the  farm,  loss  of  equipment  aggravated  the  man-
power  shortage.  In  Czechoslovakia,  25,000  citizens  responded  to  a  call
to  man  the  mines.  Bankers  and  clerks,  doctors  and  lawyers,  hauled  out
the  coal  with  hand  and  shovel.  In  Yugoslavia,  absence  of  ploughs  and

5

[PDF page 6]
tractors  threatened  food  supplies.  A  peasant  woman  ‘ploughed’  a  whole
field,  singlehanded,  with  an  axe.  2,

No  Trucks,  No  Trains
In  the  Silesian  mines,  machinery  was  intact,  but  here,  as  elsewhere,
another  ill  assailed  them.  Freight  cars  and  trucks  were  lacking.  Coal  at
the  pithead  stood  for  sale  at  360  zlotys.  In  faraway  Warsaw  it  fetched
8,000  zlotys.  Wheat,  harvested  by  hand  with  superhuman  effort,  lay
rotting  for  lack  of  transport  to  carry  it  to  areas  where  people  starved.

No  Food,  No  Clothes,  No  Shelter
Lack  of  shelter,  of  food  and  clothing  likewise  added  to  cumulative  strains,
taking  their  toll  in  sickness,  debility  and  death.  In  Yugoslavia,  one-half  a
million  homes  were  destroyed  (one  Bosnian  village,  during  the  war,  had
changed  hands  56  times).  In  Italy  400,000  people  were  without  shelter;
in  Warsaw  men  and  boys  searched  the  rubble  of  the  ruins  for  scraps  of
roofing  paper  with  which  to  cover  their  feet;  in  Greece,  more  than  half  the
population  were  still  without  minimum  clothing  needs..  From  Doboj,  in
Yugoslavia,  the  Germans  had  removed  even  swaddling  clothes,  as  padding
for  their  tanks.  Towns  and  villages  all  across  Europe  told  the  same  story,
“Nema  mishta”—there  is  nothing.

The  Crops  Fail
And,  as  though  war  and  its  aftermath  were  not  enough,  nature  conspired
to  thwart  men’s  first  painful  efforts  at  recovery.  Country  after  country  in
the  Mediterranean  basin  experienced  the  worst  drought  in  decades.  Har-
vests  fell  short  of  prewar  levels  by  50-60-70  percent.  Shortage  piled  on
shortage.  Prices  sky-rocketed  and  bewildered  men  and  women  fingered
money  that  had  lost  its  value.
Winter  Ahead
Conditions  such  as  these  persisted  into  late  summer  and  fall.  Some
became  aggravated.  And  ahead  was  winter.  The  first  frosts  came.
Villagers  in  Yugoslavia  kept  indoors  for  lack  of  footwear,  or  borrowed
from  a  neighbor.  Hospitals  had  no  heat.  In  Poland,  in  November,  a
train  steamed  in,  bringing  1,500  people  from  the  eastern  provinces.  They
had  travelled  in  open  cars  at  12  degrees  below  zero.  Six  children  froze
to  death.  In  Greece  mountain  villages  faced  the  prospect  of  complete
isolation  from  the  world  until  the  spring.  Everywhere  men  remained
preoccupied  with  bare  survival.  Recovery  was  a  mere  dream,  a  hope
deferred.

The  Two  Concurrent  Goals

The  main  objectives  of  the  quarter  were  two-fold—relief  from  the  ex-
tremes  of  present  need,  and  provision  for  the  future,  means  for  the  repair
of  industries  contributing  directly  to  relief  needs  and  for  the  recovery  of
agriculture  and  the  consequent  curtailment  of UNRRA’s  forward  liabilities.
The  more  and  the  quicker  men  helped  themselves,  the  less  and  the  shorter
the  need  for  external  assistance.
From  the  Western  Hemisphere,  food,  the  dominant,  immediate  need,
outstripped  by  far  all  other  shipments—in  October,  363,500  tons,  in Novem-
ber,  435,400  tons,  in  December,  364,000  tons.  Industrial  and  agricultural
rehabilitation  ranked  second.  Coal,  raw  materials,  and  essential  machinery
were  shipped;  tools  for  the  farmer,  tractors  and  ploughs,  basic  necessities
for  the  achievement  of  self-help  by  people  shorn  of  almost  everything  but
the  will  to  work  and  the  courage  to  survive.  Provisions  not  only  for  the  day
but  for  the  morrow—safest  insurance  against  the  unending  continuance  of
relief.  Shipment  of  these  supplies  conformed  to  a  plan  for  balanced  pro-
vision  of  relief  and  rehabilitation  supplies.  It  had  been  hoped  that,  by
the  end  of  1945,  increasing  emphasis  might  be  placed  on  the  latter.  But
between  August  and  December,  things  took  a  turn  for  the  worse.  Unan-
ticipated  world  shortages  of  wheat,  and  continuing  shortage  of  fats  and
oils  imperilled  the  relief  program.  The  continuing  urgency  of  the  demands
for  food,  fuel  and  transportation  necessitated  the  curtailment  of  supplies
of  raw  material  and  equipment  for  the  rehabilitation  of  agriculture  and
industry.  The  crisis  of  survival  was  prolonged.  Hope  of  recovery  was
again  deferred.

Gains  of  the  Quarter  Deferred

The  gains  of  the  quarter  were,  nevertheless,  decisive.  Millions  live  who,
but  for  UNRRA,  would  have  died.  The  suffering  of  further  millions  was
mitigated  by  the  provision  of  food  and  clothing,  shelter,  and  medicine.
The  importance,  moreover,  of what  has  been  averted  is  as  great  as  that  of
what  has  been  achieved.  Little  remarked,  but  of  high  significance,  is  the
total  absence  throughout  Europe  of any widespread  epidemics.  The  contrast
with  the  situation  at  the  end  of  World  War  I,  1914-1918,  is  striking.  Condi-
tions, widely  prevalent  in  almost  every  country,  were  an  open  invitation  to  in-
fection  and  the  spread  of disease.  Again  and  again,  UNRRA’s  medical  staff
~  has  helped  to  scotch  it  at  its  inception,  where  necessary,  flying  supplies  of
antitoxin,  DDT,  etc.,  by  plane  to  the  point  of  danger.  UNRRA  has
organized  the  largest  international  medical  relief  operation  in  history.  In
November  1945  there  were  800  UNRRA  physicians  and  nurses  at  work
in  Europe.
Pure  gain,  too,  has  been  the  steadily  increasing  delivery  of  rehabilitation
supplies.  While  these  have  not  always  shown  immediate  results,  they  will
earn  rich  dividends  as,  in  succeeding  months,  native  industries  increase
their  output  of basic  essential  supplies  and  the volume  of internal  trade  and  of
employment  increases,  thus  progressively  curtailing  UNRRA’s  burden  of
providing  help  from  outside  sources.  Already  countries  like  Poland  and
Czechoslovakia  have  produced  surpluses  which  they  have  made  available
for  the  relief  of  suffering  in  other  European  countries.  While  still  excep-
tional,  this  reciprocity  suggests  a  hopeful  trend.  Rewarding  dividends  will
likewise  be  paid  as,  in  springtime,  farmers  avail  themselves  of  tools  and  of
equipment  shipped  earlier  to  secure  spring  sowing.

Meanwhile  the  situation  was  further  aggravated  by  conditions  in  the
Far  East.  By  December,  rice  crops  were  known  to  be  gravely  disappointing.
With  rice  in  very  short  supply  (none  was  procurable  before  July  1945),

Eleventh  hour  advices,  further,  showed  need  for  importing  23  million  metric
tons  of rice  and/or  wheat  into Japan.
Thus  the  curve  of  demand  rose,  steeply  and  suddenly,  throughout  the
world.  These  enormous  additional  demands,  superimposed  on  crop  failures

in  1944,  and  the  short  Canadian  crop  in  1945,  resulted  in  an  ugly  gap
between  import  requirements  and  available  supplies.
On  top  of  supply  shortages  came  shipping  and  transportation  shortages.

tion,  continued  a  first  charge  on  its  operations.  The  gradual  transfer  of
emphasis  to  provision  of  agricultural  and  industrial  rehabilitation  supplies
had  to  be  deferred.  UNRRA  coatinued  locked  in  a  struggle  to  secure  sur-
vival.  It  is  against  such  facts  and  figures  that  the  achievements  of  a  record
quarter  must  be  read.  For  they  provide  an  index,  not  only  of  the  limits  of

UNRRA’s  capacity  to  help,  but  of  the  slow,  precarious  pace  of  world
recovery.
But,  beyond  countries  already  in  receipt  of  substantial  aid,  UNRRA
faced  new  extended  liabilities.  Concurrently  with  the  procurement  and
shipment  of  relief  supplies,  planning  proceeded  rapidly  for  new  and  exact-
ing  relief  and  rehabilitation  operations.

Byelorussian  and  Ukrainian  Soviet  Republics
Two  Soviet  Republics,  Byelorussia  and  the  Ukraine,  had  qualified  for
relief  assistance.  In  these  two  republics  the  destruction  of  war  had  reached
a  scale  never  before  known  in  history.  Twice  their  territories  were  a  battle-
ground—once  when  the  tide  of invasion  reached  to  Moscow  and  Stalingrad,
and  again  when  the  enemy  was  driven  out  by  the  victorious  Russian  armies.
The  enemy  removed  virtually  all  agricultural  machinery.  Livestock  was
decimated.  All  movable  stocks  of  food,  and  even  of  seeds,  were  removed.
City  after  city  was  totally  destroyed.  More  than  25,000,000  were  left
with  homes  completely  wrecked.
Forward  provision  was  made  during  the  quarter  for  relief  programs
amounting  to  $189  million  for  the  Ukraine  and  $61  million  for  Byelorussia.
First  shipments  began  before  the  end  of  the  year  (6  vessels  sailing  in  Novem-
ber,  7  in  December)  carrying  food  and  medical  supplies.  Formal  agree-
ments,  substantially  the  same  as  those  made  with  other  countries,  were
signed  on  December  18.  Under  these  agreements  the  two  Soviet  Republics
will  grant  to  UNRRA'’s  missions  privileges  and  immunities  similar  to
those  granted  to foreign  governments.  These  include  inviolability  of  the
mission’s  archives  and  premises,  exemption  from  taxes  and  immunity  from
suit  and  legal  process  with  regard  to  activities  exercised  within  the  scope
of  their  authority  under  the  agreement.  They  provide  also  for  complete
freedom  for  UNRRA  officials  to  observe  the  equitable  distribution  of
supplies  which  UNRRA  delivers.

Austria
The  extension  of  relief  operations  to  Austria  was  authorized  by  action
of  the  Council.  Late  in  the  quarter  a  formal  request,  by  the  Allied  Control
Council,  was  received  for  immediate  relief.  Conditions  in  the  country
are  desperate.  By  December  it  was  estimated  that  10,000  would  be  dying  °
of  tuberculosis  in  Vienna  alone.  UNRRA,  it  is  feared,  will  only  be  able
to  undertake  part  of  the  relief  needed  to  avert  a  tragedy.

ltaly
The  occasion  for  extended  relief  to  Italy  has  been  previously  outlined.
During  the  quarter,  plans  were  laid  and  a  draft  agreement  negotiated
with  the  Italian  Government  for  the  expansion  of  UNRRA’s  work  in  1946

# Collaborative Effort Delivers $13 Million in Critical Medical Aid to Sudan Amid Ongoing Violence

![Image 3](https://www.projecthope.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/0004_SDN_MedicalDelivery_10_2023-1-aspect-ratio-1200-675.webp)

Washington, DC – In response to the escalating violence in Sudan, [Project HOPE](https://www.projecthope.org/), [Airlink](https://airlinkflight.org/) and key partners, including [MAP International](https://www.map.org/), [Flexport.org](https://www.flexport.org/), [Astral Aviation](https://astral-aviation.com/), and [Qatar Airways](https://www.qatarairways.com/en-us/homepage.html), have successfully coordinated the delivery of $13 million (24,000 pounds) worth of vital medical supplies, pharmaceuticals, hygiene supplies, and therapeutic food to Sudan. [The Sudanese American Physicians Association (SAPA)](https://sapa-usa.org/) and Project HOPE will oversee the distribution of the shipment, ensuring that hospitals and health facilities facing the most critical shortages receive the supplies necessary to continue their vital work in treating patients.

The shipment includes essential medical supplies, ranging from syringes, gauze, and wound care items to medications, including antibiotics, antiparasitics, and pain relievers. Additionally, it includes prenatal vitamins, oral rehydration tablets, hygiene supplies, and protective equipment. Recognizing the exacerbated food insecurity across the entire Horn of Africa due to prolonged drought, the shipment also incorporates therapeutic food. The shipment will support over 100,000 people across Sudan where communities are grappling with under-resourced health facilities and cholera and dengue outbreaks.

“This shipment is a lifeline for many hospitals that are lacking the supplies and resources to address the influx of patients seeking care and lifesaving medication for everything from cholera to gunshot wounds to pregnancy,” said Arlan Fuller, Director of Emergency Preparedness and Response for Project HOPE. “This partnership exemplifies the essence of humanitarianism — nonprofits and corporations coming together to share resources and knowledge to reach those who need support the most.”

“Airlink’s partners have struggled to get needed medical aid into Sudan since the conflict broke out in April, owing to the limited flight options and high cost of airlift into Port Sudan – the country’s only operating airport. We are proud to say, we’ve found a way to get aid there,” said Steve Smith, Airlink President & CEO. “By bringing together our donors and partners in the private sector – Astral Aviation, Flexport.org, and Qatar Airways Cargo – and coordinating this shipment with long-time nonprofit partner Project HOPE, we’ve been able to make the impossible possible in the midst of one of the most challenging humanitarian crises facing the world. We hope this is just the start of our work in Sudan, breaking down the logistical barriers to get aid where it is needed most.”

“MAP International’s participation in this collaborative effort to deliver $13 million in critical medical aid to Sudan underscores our commitment to making a meaningful impact on global health crises. In timesof escalating violence and dire need, it is imperative that organizations and partners unite to provide essential medical supplies, pharmaceuticals, and support to vulnerable communitie,” said Steve Stirling, President and CEO, MAP International. “Together with our dedicated partners, we are honored to be a part of this vital mission, which will help save lives and alleviate suffering in Sudan and the Horn of Africa.”

“SAPA is honored to continue supporting health personnel in Sudan who have been working tirelessly to provide essential medical services. This shipment will ensure that hospitals and doctors on the ground are able to obtain the supplies necessary to carry out their incredible work,” said Dr. Yasir Elamin, President of SAPA. “We are grateful for the opportunity to collaborate with Project HOPE and so many incredible partners to deliver much-needed medical aid to the region.”

“Flexport.org is thankful for our strong partnerships that enable the effective and efficient delivery of lifesaving humanitarian aid, and to our donors like Tech For Refugees, a non-profit that supports refugee relief efforts through technology,” Kristen Czapar Dohnt, Head of Flexport.org.

“Astral Aviation is proud of its association with Airlink and to be of service to its partners by providing a dedicated charter from its Nairobi Hub to Port Sudan on the Boeing 727F with 10782 kgs of humanitarian cargoes,” said Mike Mutahi, Chief Operating Officer of Astral Aviation. “Astral Aviation will continue to cooperate with our partners in delivering humanitarian cargoes to regions in Africa and Middle East with its dedicated fleet and expertise.”

Photos are available [here](https://projecthope.canto.com/s/N2OSO?viewIndex=1). To schedule an interview, please contact [media@projecthope.org](mailto:media@projecthope.org).

###

**About Project HOPE**  
Founded in 1958, Project HOPE is a leading global health and humanitarian organization operating in more than 20 countries around the world. We respond to emergencies and work side-by-side with local health systems to improve health outcomes. For more information on Project HOPE and its work around the world, visit www.ProjectHOPE.org and follow us on Twitter and Instagram @ProjectHOPEorg.

**About Airlink**  
Airlink is a nonprofit organization providing free air transport and logistical coordination for pre-screened nonprofits to deliver disaster responders and supplies in the wake of humanitarian crises worldwide. Its network includes over 200 aid organizations and 50 air carriers and logistics partners. Its first mission was in response to the Haiti earthquake. Since its inception in 2010, Airlink’s airline partners have flown more than 11,000 relief workers and transported 12 million pounds of humanitarian cargo, saving nonprofits over $33 million in air transport costs, directly helping over 46 million people. In addition, Airlink receives in-kind gifts from airlines and donations from organizations and individuals within the aviation sector. For more information, visit www.airlinkflight.org.

**About MAP International**  
MAP International is a non-profit global health organization dedicated to providing medicine for all people. With a strong focus on delivering medical aid in times of crisis, MAP International works collaboratively with partners and donors to improve the health and well-being of communities facing significant challenges. Through our mission-driven approach, we strive to make a positive impact on the lives of those in need, particularly in regions experiencing conflict and humanitarian emergencies. Learn more about our work at www.map.org.

**About Flexport.org**Flexport.org is the dedicated sustainability and impact team within Flexport that enables organizations to deliver aid and meet their decarbonization goals with greater ease and lower costs. Flexport.org creates value-added services for Flexport users to measure and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, bringing sustainability into the forefront of their business roadmap. Flexport.org also provides critically needed visibility and expertise to nonprofits and NGOs, governments, and social enterprises, helping deliver humanitarian aid, disaster relief and development shipments where they are needed most. To date, we have delivered over 74 million pounds of aid in 3,984 shipments, impacting 120 million people globally. For more information, visit www.flexport.org.

**About Astral Aviation**Astral Aviation is a dedicated cargo airline which is based at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport in Nairobi, Kenya, and operates a fleet of 15 cargo aircrafts to over 50 destinations in Africa, from its hubs in Nairobi, Johannesburg, Liege, Dubai and Hong Kong. Celebrating its 23rd Anniversary in 2023, Astral is the fastest growing Cargo Airline in Africa with a diversified fleet capacity which ranges from 5 tons to 110 tons and has recently taken delivery of its Boeing 757-200 Freighter. For media information: Astral Aviation Media Relations – [https://www.astral-aviation.com/news/](https://www.astral-aviation.com/news/)

**About SAPA**  
The Sudanese American Physicians Association (SAPA) is a nonprofit, professional, non-partisan, and humanitarian organization operating in Sudan since 2019. Visit[www.sapa-usa.org](https://www.sapa-usa.org/) and follow us on X (twitter) @sapa_org
